summary: Physicists at IHEP and Jilin University define HepScript, a Ruby-embedded DSL that a processor turns into BESIII BOSS and ROOT analysis code. LLMs are prompted with one long example plus a YARD grammar to emit HepScript from published papers, then retried on processor errors. The evaluation is 45 filtered BESIII papers and two full ROOT case studies.

claims.claim: HepScript reduces human-written analysis code by 93%
claims.evidence: §5.3: character count, comments and blanks excluded, averaged over two case studies (J/psi and psi-prime). No per-case counts, no time-on-task, and no comparison with writing the same analysis in Python or C++ without the DSL.

claims.claim: Agents generate executable specifications for core stages from the literature with about a 95% success rate
claims.evidence: Table 1, LLM-generated block: DeepSeek-R1 34/72 packages (47.3%) and GLM-4.7 31/72 (43.2%) on the first try; after three error-feedback retries 94.6±2.6% and 95.9±2.3%. Scope is dataset preparation and base selection only (72 packages), not the full five-stage workflow. Logical correctness is an unblinded expert judgment with no agreement statistic. Binomial standard errors are uncertainty on one run, not repeated seeds.

claims.claim: A constrained DSL makes generation reliable where open-ended framework code would not
claims.evidence: No arm generates BOSS or ROOT code directly from the same papers. The one-shot versus retry comparison isolates the feedback loop, not the DSL. Semantic RAG is abandoned in §4.1 with no measured comparison.

claims.claim: The processor's deterministic core is sound, and LLM-assisted variable storage reaches 98.5% after one retry
claims.evidence: Table 1, human-written block: 63 packages compile with the LLM component off; with it on, one-retry success is 98.5±1.5% for all five models. DeepSeek-R1's first-try 87.7% includes four timeouts. This checks the translator on expert-written specs, not generation from papers.

claims.claim: Generated ROOT scripts reproduce published figures
claims.evidence: Fig. 3: two analyses, visual comparison only. §5.4 says full execution was limited to these two cases because of dataset cost, and the figures are not official physics results.

patterns.note: HepScript is a machine-readable grammar for one experiment's analysis stages. The paper never compares that grammar with free-form prompts or an existing HEP DSL on the same papers.

On the 72 generated packages, feeding processor errors back raises package success from 43–47% to about 95% after three retries (Table 1). The alternative is the same prompt with no retry. Remaining failures are multi-error cases, and success mixes compile with expert logic review.
The architecture is spec-then-generate: HepScript is the specification and the processor emits BOSS, ROOT, and shell. There is no head-to-head with generating the target code directly.
§2.1 says experts can trace generated code back to the HepScript file. That property is not measured.
An agentic memory of past specifications is proposed in §6.3 and not built.

methodology.sample: First 50 BESIII arXiv papers by date, filtered by DeepSeek-V3 to 45 whose methods fit the current grammar; one expert writes each ground-truth spec and a second checks it. Generation scored on dataset preparation and base selection (72 packages). ROOT execution on 2 analyses.
methodology.baselines: One-shot generation versus one and three retries with error text. Human-written specs as a processor check. No direct-code-generation arm and no semantic-RAG arm.
methodology.models: DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-4o, GLM-4.7, Qwen3-Max for processor-side translation; only DeepSeek-R1 and GLM-4.7 for paper-to-HepScript generation
methodology.variance: Bayesian binomial standard errors on a single pass per package. No seeds.
methodology.ablations: LLM-assisted variable storage on versus off for human specs. No ablation of the DSL, the long prompt, or the grammar reference.
methodology.contamination_controls: None. DeepSeek-V3 both filters the corpus and is a model under test. Papers are public and likely in pretraining data.
methodology.languages: Ruby DSL emitting C++ (BOSS), ROOT/C++, Bash, and some Python. Not Java.

standards.artifacts: Prompt reproduced in Appendix D. No code, grammar package, or 45-spec corpus release found.

biases.detail: Coding-effort reduction is non-comment character count on two pipelines, not developer time or defect rate.
Papers whose methods exceed the grammar (deep learning, cross-sections, amplitude analyses) are removed before scoring, so the 95% rate is on workflows the DSL was built to express.
Full execution and the 93% figure rest on two analyses. Generation uses two models.
One generation per paper. The ± figures are binomial uncertainty, not reruns.
Processor, specs, and prompts beyond the appendix are not released.
The abstract's 95% success and 'rendering previously intractable automation problems solvable' describe a partial pipeline after three retries, starting from about 45%.

verdict_reason: Off-topic. This is a BESIII analysis DSL, not software development, onboarding, or codebase exploration. The retry loop is a real measurement (about 45% to about 95% on 72 partial-stage packages), but the 93% effort cut is two character-count case studies, the DSL itself is not compared with direct code generation, and nothing is released.
applicability: It does not transfer to the Java multi-repo team. The language, runtime, and success metric are experiment-specific particle-physics workflows. A shared grammar can be a domain contract in principle, but this paper does not show that such a contract beats ordinary code generation, and the team's ingestion services are not a single Ruby DSL over one stack.
